examples.question_text: A shape has area $27\text{ cm}^{2}$. Mia cuts it into pieces and makes a rectangle. Leo uses an identical set of pieces to make an irregular shape. Each uses every piece once without overlap. What is the area of each arrangement? Explain.
examples.solution_text: Both arrangements have area $27\text{ cm}^{2}$. Cutting and moving the pieces changes their arrangement, but adds or removes no surface. The different outlines do not change the total covered area.

examples.question_text: All the pieces from a $32\text{ cm}^{2}$ shape are rearranged. Two pieces overlap over an area of $7\text{ cm}^{2}$, and there is no other overlap. Find the total area of the pieces and the area visibly covered.
examples.solution_text:
The pieces still total $32\text{ cm}^{2}$. The overlap is counted twice in that total but covered only once, so subtract it once.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}32-7\\&=25\end{aligned}$

The arrangement visibly covers $25\text{ cm}^{2}$.

examples.question_text: Pieces with total area $26\text{ cm}^{2}$ are arranged without overlap inside an outline. The only uncovered region inside the outline is a $5\text{ cm}^{2}$ gap. Find the area of the pieces and the area enclosed by the outline.
examples.solution_text:
The pieces have area $26\text{ cm}^{2}$. The outline encloses the pieces and the gap, so add their areas.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}26+5\\&=31\end{aligned}$

The outline encloses $31\text{ cm}^{2}$. The gap is not covered by a piece.

examples.question_text: A puzzle uses eight pieces to make a rectangle. Another design uses only seven of those pieces, without overlap. Can its covered area equal the rectangle's area? Explain.
examples.solution_text: No. The omitted piece has positive area. Translating, reflecting or rotating the seven remaining pieces preserves their sizes, so their total covered area stays smaller than the eight-piece rectangle's area.

examples.derivation: The diagonals intersect at (2.5, 1.5), forming four triangular regions, one beside each rectangle side. The solution labels identify those four regions correctly.

The cut triangle has vertices (0,0), (1,0), (1,3). Translating it five units right gives (5,0), (6,0), (6,3), filling the right-hand gap. The union is the rectangle from (1,0) to (6,3); the dashed seam and T label agree.

A half-turn followed by translation maps the second triangle to vertices (5,2), (1,2), (4,0). It joins the first along (4,0)–(1,2). The outer boundary has opposite side vectors (4,0) and (1,2), forming a parallelogram without overlap.

The cut at x=4 separates rectangles measuring 4 by 3 and 3 by 1. A quarter-turn makes the detached piece 1 by 3; placing it beside the larger rectangle forms a 5 by 3 rectangle. Both arrangements have area 12+3=15 square units.
Each arrangement uses an identical complete set of pieces once without overlap. Their covered areas therefore both equal the original 27 square centimetres, regardless of outline.

Total piece area remains 32 square centimetres. The sole two-piece overlap contributes one extra count of 7 square centimetres, so visible coverage is 32−7=25 square centimetres. The continuation calculation has the required phantom equals gutter.

Non-overlapping pieces cover 26 square centimetres. Adding the only uncovered interior region gives enclosed area 26+5=31 square centimetres. The continuation calculation has the required phantom equals gutter.
Removing one positive-area piece reduces the sum of piece areas. Rigid movements preserve each remaining piece's area, and non-overlap makes covered area equal that smaller sum.
